list-item.p: High ALC after cilta-cel treatment are associated with high risk of mortality and atypical neurologic events.
Patients with elevated ALC who received 3 days of dexamethasone prophylaxis tended to have fewer neurologic events and lower mortality.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Increased absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) may predict risk of treatment-related mortality and atypical neurologic events among patients receiving chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapies for relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma. In this study, we analyzed the clinical outcomes of patients receiving ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel) at the Colorado Blood Cancer Institute, from September 2023 to January 2025. Baseline data were collected pre/post-CAR T-cell therapy. Patients were stratified into preintervention (treated September 2023 to July 2024) and intervention (treated August 2024 to January 2025; those with ALC >5 × 103/μL received 3 days of dexamethasone prophylaxis on first identification of elevated ALC). In the preintervention group, 9 of 30 patients had peak ALC >5 × 103/μL; 5 of 9 (55.6%) experienced atypical neurologic events and all 5 died (cilta-cel therapy-related complications). In the intervention group, 7 of 23 patients had peak ALC >5 × 103/μL and received dexamethasone; 1 of 7 had an atypical neurologic event; and 1 death occured (infectious complication, 9 months posttreatment). Dexamethasone prophylaxis in patients with ALC of >5 × 103/μL resulted in rapid ALC reduction. Overall survival (OS) was significantly lower in preintervention patients with ALC of >5 × 103/μL vs intervention patients with ALC of >5 × 103/μL and patients with ALC of ≤5 × 103/μL (P = .0013). ALC >5 × 103/μL (vs ALC ≤ 5 × 103/μL) was significantly associated with atypical neurologic events (odds ratio, 6.8; P = .0157) and lower OS (hazard ratio, 6.2; P = .0106). In conclusion, ALC >5 × 103/μL after cilta-cel treatment predicted severe early neurologic events and high mortality risk. Dexamethasone prophylaxis demonstrated promise for risk mitigation.

sec.p: Received 2025 Oct 22; Accepted 2026 Mar 6; Collection date 2026 May 26.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapies have shown remarkable efficacy in the treatment of patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (RRMM). However, a subset of patients experience immune-related adverse reactions and even treatment-related mortality following CAR T-cell therapy.1, 2, 3, 4 These events include immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) and non-ICANS or atypical neurologic events,5 which are CAR T-cell–related neurologic events that do not fit the current definition of ICANS.

Ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel), a B-cell maturation antigen–directed CAR T-cell therapy, has demonstrated marked and durable responses in both heavily pretreated patients with RRMM and those with lenalidomide-refractory disease in earlier lines of therapy (LOT).1,2,6,7 However, atypical immune and/or neurologic events have been observed in patients treated with cilta-cel. The reported spectrum of non-ICANS neurologic events described after cilta-cel therapy is diverse and includes movement and neurocognitive treatment-emergent events or immune effector cell–parkinsonism, cognitive impairment or personality changes, peripheral neuropathy, and cranial nerve palsies (CNPs).8 The mechanism of these complications is not well understood and their incidence rates in real-world clinical practice have been reported in few studies.3,4,9 Additionally, the mortality associated with some of these complications can be significant, and current approaches to treat the more complex cases effectively remain limited. Finally, a recent study following real-world cilta-cel or idecabtagene vicleucel treatment showed intrinsic biological differences between these 2 B-cell maturation antigen–directed CAR T-cell therapies, potentially explaining the differences in clinical activity and toxicity.10

Given that cilta-cel has shown deep and durable responses in patients with RRMM, there is an urgent need to identify patients at risk for severe neurologic events and nonrelapse-related mortality and to develop and integrate risk-mitigation strategies. Our group performed a preliminary analysis of patients treated with cilta-cel at the Colorado Blood Cancer Institute (CBCI), and we identified degree of absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) expansion after CAR T-cell administration as a strong predictor of risk for non-ICANS neurologic events and increased treatment-related mortality.11 ALC and CAR+ T-cell counts are significantly correlated at and around peak expansion, and ALC represents an early and readily available biomarker for monitoring CAR T-cell activity following cilta-cel treatment.12 Overall, patients with excessive CAR T-cell expansion may be at risk for subsequent immune-mediated or non-ICANS neurologic events and represent an opportunity for early identification of patients at risk with tailored interventions to improve safety. We developed a preventive strategy to monitor ALC expansion and use dexamethasone initiated at first identification of excessive lymphocyte expansion (ALC > 5 × 103/μL) to mitigate treatment-related toxicity.

In this study, we analyzed the clinical outcomes from patients with RRMM who were treated with cilta-cel at the CBCI. To determine possible interventions to mitigate and reduce risk, predictors for immune-related and atypical (non-ICANS) neurologic events were evaluated. Excessive ALC expansion post cilta-cel infusion was a predictive factor for severe neurologic events and high mortality risk. A protocol for preemptive dexamethasone initiated at early evidence of excessive ALC emergence was identified as a promising strategy to mitigate this risk without compromising antitumor efficacy.

sec.title: Study design and patients
sec.p: A retrospective review was conducted on patients who were treated with cilta-cel at the CBCI between September 2023 and January 2025. Baseline demographics, disease characteristics, and clinical data were collected for patients before and after CAR T-cell therapy.

Following an internal process improvement review in July 2024, patients who developed ALC >5 × 103/μL during the first 30 days following CAR T-cell administration were treated with dexamethasone prophylaxis. Patients treated from September 2023 to July 2024 (preintervention group) with ALC >5 × 103/μL had no preventive intervention, and patients treated from August 2024 to January 2025 (intervention group) with ALC >5 × 103/μL were treated with dexamethasone prophylaxis on first identification of elevated lymphocyte expansion. The 30-day window was chosen to align with when patients were monitored at the CBCI, before potentially transitioning care back to their home oncologist’s clinic. Dexamethasone was dosed at 10 mg every 8 hours on day 1, every 12 hours on day 2, then once on day 3, and then discontinued. The dexamethasone dosing strategy was informed by dosing schemas for dexamethasone used for the management of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and ICANS.

Additionally, at the time of process improvement, a more stringent approach to bridging therapy during CAR T-cell manufacturing was adopted: all patients in the intervention group received bridging therapy prioritizing achievement of a measurable response (partial response or better) before CAR T-cell administration and intensive bridging therapy (characterized as talquetamab or infusional chemotherapy such as DCEP [dexamethasone, cyclophosphamide, etoposide, and cisplatin]/PACE [cisplatin, adriamycin/doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, and etoposide]). sec.title: Adverse events
sec.p: The primary outcomes of interest were death and atypical (non-ICANS) neurologic events. Several independent variables were evaluated for association with the primary outcomes (Table 2).

sec.title: Statistical methods
sec.p: Categorial variables were tested for association with intervention status using a χ2 test or Fisher exact test when cell sizes were small. Continuous variables were tested for association with intervention status using an analysis of variance. Logistic regression analyses were used to compute odds ratios for variables of interest. SAS version 9.4 was used for analysis. Kaplan-Meier methods were used to create survival curves. The log-rank test was used to compare differences in median overall survival (OS) based on intervention status.

sec.title: ALC expansion and OS
sec.p: To investigate cilta-cel immune effector adverse effects, a total of 53 patients treated with cilta-cel were examined in this analysis, with a median follow-up of 371 days from their CAR T-cell treatment. Patient characteristics are summarized in Table 1. The cohort had a median age of 66 years (range, 41-80), and 47.2% of patients (25) were female. Most characteristics were similar across the nonintervention and intervention groups. However, there were differences in cytogenetic abnormalities and prior therapies. A higher percentage of the intervention group than the nonintervention group had t(4;14) and gain(1q) mutations and received prior carfilzomib and bispecific treatment. Because of the stringent approach to bridging therapy adopted after July 2024, there were also significant differences between the nonintervention and intervention groups in bridging therapies and bridging response when entering CAR T-cell treatment. A higher percentage of the intervention group than the nonintervention group received intensive bridging treatment (47.8 vs 13.3%; P = .0087) and were definitively responding to bridging (65.2 vs 16.7%; P < .0001) when entering CAR T-cell treatment. Despite the timing of the intervention being implemented shortly after the approval of cilta-cel in April 2024 for use in earlier lines for RRMM, there was no significant difference in median LOT received by patients in the nonintervention and intervention groups (both 4).

Patients represent a real-world population treated at a single US medical center during the study. The median peak ALC was 3.2 × 103/μL. Across the full cohort, 16 patients (30.2%) developed peak ALC expansion >5 × 103/μL. For patients in the preintervention group (received cilta-cel between September 2023 and July 2024), 9 of 30 (30.0%) developed a peak ALC >5 × 103/μL; 5 of 9 (55.6%) experienced atypical neurologic events, and all 5 patients died of complications related to cilta-cel treatment. In the intervention group (patients who received cilta-cel between August 2024 and January 2025), 7 of 23 patients (30.4%) developed a peak ALC >5 × 103/μL, all of whom received ALC-directed dexamethasone prophylaxis. Only 1 of 7 of these patients experienced an atypical neurologic event, and the only death in this cohort was due to an infectious complication 9 months after CAR T-cell treatment.

ALC kinetics for patients over the initial 30 days following CAR T-cell administration are presented in Figure 1. All patients experienced an initial rise in their ALC count around day +11 after receiving CAR T-cell therapy. In patients who did not develop atypical neurologic events this expansion was generally brief with a lower peak ALC level and a quick reduction to their subsequent baseline ALC (Figure 1A). Patients who developed eventual atypical neurologic events experienced a more dramatic and sustained ALC expansion (Figure 1A). Patients who had an ALC >5 × 103/μL who received dexamethasone demonstrated a quick correction to day +14 lymphocyte counts consistent with patients who had a lower peak ALC count (Figure 1B). In contrast, patients whose ALC rose to >5 × 103/μL before initiation of ALC-directed dexamethasone prophylaxis experienced a higher peak and more sustained ALC elevation (Figure 1B).

sec.p: The median follow-up for patients with peak ALC >5 × 103/μL who received ALC-directed dexamethasone was 329 days (range, 109-350); for those with peak ALC >5 × 103/μL who did not receive ALC-directed dexamethasone was 446 days (range, 375-507); and for those with peak ALC ≤5 × 103/μL, it was 371 days (range, 290-494). Median OS from cilta-cel infusion for patients with peak ALC ≤5 × 103/μL was not estimable (95% confidence interval [CI], not reached [NR]). Median OS for patients with peak ALC >5 × 103/μL who received ALC-directed dexamethasone was also not estimable (95% CI, NR), compared with a median OS of 104 days (95% CI, 27 to NR) in those with no ALC-directed dexamethasone (Figure 2A). Progression-free survival for patients is illustrated in Figure 2B.

caption.p: Kaplan-Meier curves for survival. (A) OS; (B) PFS. Curves show survival estimates, with number of patients at risk and 95% Hall-Wellner bands. “Intervention” indicates ALC-directed dexamethasone prophylaxis. NE, not estimable; PFS, progression-free survival.

sec.p: Across the full cohort, 36 of 51 evaluable patients (70.6%) achieved a documented complete response (CR) following bridging and CAR T-cell therapy (Table 2), and the proportion of patients achieving CR was no different before the implementation of ALC-directed dexamethasone therapy (preintervention group; 19/28 evaluable patients, 67.9%) or after (intervention group; 17/23 patients, 73.9%). In the intervention group, 9 patients received dexamethasone based on ALC expansion, all 9 achieved a best response of a CR or better. At time of data cutoff, only 1 of these 9 patients had experienced disease progression, whereas another died of infectious complication without experiencing disease progression. Although long-term efficacy data continue to mature, no differences in depth or durability of response in patients treated with ALC-directed dexamethasone were identified in our cohort. Comparisons are further limited by differences in follow-up time between the preintervention and intervention groups.

sec.title: Clinical correlates associated with peak ALC expansion >5 × 103/μL
sec.p: Several factors were significantly associated with a peak ALC expansion threshold of 5 × 103/μL. These included Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status at cilta-cel infusion, development of CRS, highest grade of CRS, dexamethasone or other glucocorticoid treatment for CRS/ICANS, tocilizumab treatment for CRS/ICANS, anakinra treatment for CRS/ICANS, and highest grade of ICANS (Table 2). Notable factors that were not found to have a statistically significant association with ALC expansion >5 × 103/μL included size of last M-protein or degree of effected light chain elevation before CAR T-cell therapy administration, response to bridging therapy, intensive vs nonintensive bridging therapy, number of prior LOT, or specific historical treatment exposures.

The only correlates found to have a statistically significant impact on the likelihood of death (Figure 3) were peak ALC expansion >5 × 103/μL vs ALC ≤5 × 103/μL (hazard ratio [HR], 6.2; P = .0106), the development of an atypical neurologic event (HR, 21.3; P < .0001), and the achievement of a CR or better (HR, 0.130; P = .0148). There was a notable trend toward lower mortality in all patients treated after August 2024, when ALC-directed dexamethasone prophylaxis and more stringent bridging therapy were instituted (intervention vs preintervention; HR, 0.221; P = .1627).8 ALC expansion was the only correlate found to have a statistically significant impact on the likelihood of developing atypical neurologic events (odds ratio, 6.8; P = .0157; Figure 4).

sec.p: Patients who did not receive prophylactic dexamethasone experienced more severe non-ICANS neurologic events. This included 2 patients who developed parkinsonism, both of whom died due to uncontrolled infection following significant immunosuppressive therapy. Two additional patients developed CNP: 1 experienced subsequent progressive deterioration in clinical/neurologic status with broader symptoms including dysphagia, weakness, altered mental status, progressive confusion, and gait and balance worsening; the other experienced progressive confusion, and gait and balance dysfunction. A fifth patient developed confusion and general decline in neurologic status. In comparison, there were only 3 patients with atypical neurologic events following the introduction of prophylactic dexamethasone, and they each developed isolated cranial nerve VII palsies, which fully resolved in all patients. These CNPs developed on day +22 and day +23 in patients who started dexamethasone on days +9 and +11, respectively. One CNP developed on day +18 in a patient who did not receive dexamethasone as their peak ALC was <5 × 103/μL.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Results from the CARTITUDE-1 and CARTITUDE-4 trials have clearly demonstrated that cilta-cel represents a highly effective treatment option for patients with RRMM.1,2,6,7 However, atypical immune-related and non-ICANS neurologic events have been reported following cilta-cel.5 As cilta-cel moves into earlier LOT, the potential for high-risk complications needs to be balanced against the survival benefit. It is important to characterize risk factors associated with non-ICANS neurologic events, or early CAR T-cell–associated mortality that can be readily identified in routine clinical practice.

Our evaluation of patients treated in a real-world setting with cilta-cel identified that patients who experienced restrained ALC expansion ≤5 × 103/μL after cilta-cel infusion had better survival and less severe immune-related and atypical neurologic events. Excessive ALC expansion, with ALC rising to >5 × 103/μL early following cilta-cel infusion, resulted in increased nonrelapse-related mortality and a higher rate and greater severity of non-ICANS neurologic events. The intervention adopted in response to this observation, using 3 days of prophylactic dexamethasone in patients with ALC expansion >5 × 103/μL early after infusion, appeared to improve immune-related events and patient outcomes.

In our analysis, we observed that excessive ALC expansion is a reliable predictor of atypical (non-ICANS) neurologic events. Similar findings have been described in a recent analysis conducted of patients treated with cilta-cel for RRMM across the CARTITUDE trials.12 In these trials, ALC and CAR+ T-cell counts were observed to be significantly correlated at and around peak expansion, with heightened CAR+ T-cell levels after infusion likely being associated with the development of parkinsonism and CNP. A multivariate analysis identified elevated ALC, CAR+ T-cell peak expansion, and CD4 T-cell counts early following cilta-cel infusion as factors associated with higher risk of atypical neurologic events, with ALC demonstrating the strongest predictive value.12 The correlation of ALC with atypical neurologic events including parkinsonism and CNPs was also seen in a retrospective analysis of patients with MM who received cilta-cel as standard of care at the Mayo Clinic.13 Overall, these data, considered together with the results reported here, highlight the importance of monitoring ALC, which is an early and readily available biomarker to identify patients with higher risk of atypical neurologic events.

To date, strategies to manage atypical neurologic events after cilta-cel administration have been adopted to alter symptom trajectory after pathophysiologic processes are underway. These include potentially toxic or invasive therapies such as high-dose cyclophosphamide and intrathecal methotrexate.8,14 The ALC-directed intervention described here with low-dose, fixed-duration dexamethasone early in the postinfusion period offers a potential preemptive approach to reduce the risk for severe immune or neurologic injury. The ALC trajectory following dexamethasone appeared to demonstrate a rapid reduction toward a more routine expansion trajectory and a less prolonged exposure to an excessively expanded CAR T-cell population. In our limited cohort, following intervention, not only were patients less likely to develop atypical neurologic events, but such events were also less severe. Without intervention, patients who developed severe neurologic events often ultimately progressed to experience nonrelapse mortality. There was a trend toward improvement in mortality following development of this intervention across the full cohort. Following the incorporation in ALC-directed dexamethasone, there was no difference in the rate of CR and no apparent difference in progression-free survival compared with patients who did not receive preventive dexamethasone. Long-term outcomes data for this cohort are not yet available.

Notably, dexamethasone prophylaxis for ALC expansion as administered in our patient cohort did not appear to prevent CNPs. Recent data from the Mayo Clinic have demonstrated that the elevated lymphocyte expansion associated with CNPs may be lower than the expansion associated with parkinsonism and other events.13 This would suggest that to further reduce risk for these events as well, use of a lower ALC expansion threshold of >3 × 103/μL may be preferable to the 5 × 103/μL threshold in our initial intervention. It is also possible that CNPs have a pathophysiology distinct from other forms of atypical neurologic events, and CNPs may be less affected by dexamethasone prophylaxis. Reassuringly, all patients who developed Bell’s palsy in our cohort following dexamethasone intervention achieved full symptomatic recovery.

Bridging therapy and its effectiveness also appears to have a substantial impact on the development of atypical neurologic events and the overall safety following cilta-cel administration.15 Greater response to bridging therapy has already been correlated with improved efficacy.16 We found that mortality tended to be lower in patients with a response to bridging therapy than in patients with only stable response or those actively progressing despite bridging. These data emphasize the importance of optimizing bridging therapy for appropriate disease control and heightened responses before cilta-cel infusion. More efficacious or intensive bridging therapy did not correlate to a reduction in the likelihood for excessive ALC expansion. The difference in bridging intensity and efficacy in patients adopted concurrently with ALC-directed dexamethasone is one of the primary limitations of this analysis in delineating the specific impact of either intervention in isolation. Rather than considering the impact of either ALC-directed dexamethasone or stringent bridging alone as an approach to improve safety of cilta-cel administration, the impact on OS and atypical neurologic events described in our analysis is best interpreted as an outcome of both interventions in parallel. Our findings warrant further investigation using larger cohorts to examine ALC-directed dexamethasone and stringent bridging approaches in isolation.

In conclusion, excessive ALC expansion (>5 × 103/μL) after cilta-cel predicted severe early atypical (non-ICANS) neurologic events and high mortality risk. The use of prophylactic dexamethasone showed promise to mitigate this risk without an identifiable impact on efficacy of therapy. Use of a standardized protocol for prophylactic management of emerging excessive ALC with dexamethasone 10 mg every 8 hours on day 1, followed by 10 mg every 12 hours on day 2, and 10 mg once on day 3 was straightforward, low toxicity, and easy to implement into routine after CAR T-cell therapy management in our center. This type of consistent approach offers a low-cost, easily accessible intervention that may improve safety for patients undergoing cilta-cel therapy. Further prospective analysis of prophylactic dexamethasone for ALC expansion in formalized, prospective clinical trials is warranted based on these initial findings.
